title: Who Leads the Governance Rebuild?
say: Welcome. This is the executive briefing for Book 01 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, The Transformation Arc. It runs about thirty minutes, and it's for the people who sponsor, fund, secure and authorize the move from a domain-joined estate to cloud identity, cloud device management and governed hybrid operations. The argument fits in three sentences. For twenty years Active Directory quietly did governance nobody wrote down, so modernization is a governance rebuild, not a platform swap. The estate has to be analyzed before anything moves, and the work delivered in gated phases with a rollback at every step. And leadership's job is to conduct the orchestra, not to play the instruments. I'll cover why this is hard, what changes, who leads, and how to deliver it, all the way to the retirement of Active Directory. There's no configuration on these slides. Each decision slide names the decision, who owns it, and when it's needed. Let's start with how the estate got here.

title: Every new mandate assumes a foundation never built
say: Federal IT reached its current shape in four eras, and each one solved a real problem. The mainframe held the data and enforced access to it: one truth, in one box. Distributed systems put a database and a directory in every region, and nobody replaced that single truth. Then email and workloads moved to the cloud while identity stayed in regional domains. Now the same person can appear as several records, and no one can say which is authoritative. That's why modernization stalls. Each step assumes the one before it is finished. Zero Trust assumes authoritative cloud identity, which assumes a clean directory, which assumes governed groups, which assume someone owns them. That last step is where many agencies are stuck. Meanwhile the mandates arrive with dates, and each assumes a foundation the estate never built. So the first decision is about ownership, not technology. Before anything is planned, name the executive sponsor, the steward who runs the program office, and the authorizing official. The roadmap makes that the entry condition for its first phase. Next, the problem in precise terms.

title: Active Directory was the governance nobody wrote down
say: Active Directory shipped with Windows 2000 as an identity directory. Over twenty-five years every Windows-era service wired itself into it, because it was the only governed, replicated namespace available. Nobody wrote down how much governance it carried. The OU tree wasn't a folder system. Placing one user in a branch set their administrators, their Group Policy, their groups, their delegation and their audit boundary. One act, five effects. Entra ID has no OU tree, so each effect has to be rebuilt on purpose. Most migration plans count users, computers, groups and Group Policy. The program counts eleven categories, adding service accounts, DNS and DHCP, certificate services, RADIUS, LDAP-bound applications and trusts. Those fail silently. No log line says governance has failed. Microsoft hasn't deprecated Active Directory, so there's no vendor deadline; retiring it is the agency's decision. That makes scope a decision for the sponsor and the CIO, when scope and funding are set: fund this as a governance transformation across all eleven categories, not a users-and-groups project. Next, what has to be true for the target to hold.

title: Five things must be true before the target holds
say: The workbook reads federal Zero Trust guidance as requiring five things. No single document publishes this list; it's the program's synthesis. One authoritative source of identity. A governed directory, rationalized before the move, not after. Continuous verification, not one-time sign-in. Telemetry used for management, not only incident response. And governance that runs automatically, because manual review can't keep up. Continuous verification is where old and new differ most. In Active Directory a user signs in once and gets a ticket that lasts ten hours, renewable for seven days. In Entra ID an access token lasts one hour by default, and under continuous access evaluation it can be revoked within about fifteen minutes of an event such as a disabled account. Distance matters, but narrowly. It hurts the operations that still need a domain controller, like sign-in and policy on hybrid-joined devices. Light in fiber from Portland, Oregon to Washington takes about forty-five milliseconds round trip, and bandwidth doesn't change that. The durable answer is to remove the dependency. Now, what changes, starting with the platform.

title: Platform: one governed host, one authoritative writer
say: The platform is the one place where every decision is written down, signed and replayable. The reference design runs every analysis, plan and evidence step on one Windows Server 2025 host, with a standby for recovery. What matters is a single authoritative writer, because two writers would diverge. Every change is a signed commit, never a portal click. Two rules matter at this level. First, governance and execution never mix. One layer validates and signs plans but never touches a target; the other runs authorized plans and decides nothing. They run under separate identities, because a component that both decides and acts can cover its tracks. Second, the host reads the forest and writes to cloud identity, so it's treated as Tier 0. The program's target posture for federal production is gated actuation: the host proposes a correction, and a person approves it before it runs. The decision belongs to the program office, under the steward: stand up the host as the only authoritative writer, protected as Tier 0, and record the standby model and actuation stage. Gate G0 needs it operational by the end of Phase 0. Next, identity.

title: Identity: the attributes have to be true first
say: Identity comes first, because policy, devices and access all target identity groups. The OU tree carried delegation, policy scope and accountability in one structure. A flat cloud directory has none of that until the program writes it down. The book rebuilds it with attributes, dynamic groups, administrative units and Conditional Access. Setting a user's attributes from the HR record drives group membership, delegated scope, policy, licenses and drift visibility. One stamp, five outcomes. That only works if the attributes are true. For the workforce, the authoritative source is the HR system of record. A dynamic rule is only as trustworthy as whoever can write the attribute it reads, so the help-desk and self-service write paths are removed, and HR provisioning becomes the only writer. Tokens don't fix a wrong model; they sign broken authorizations efficiently. So HR decides what the authoritative attributes mean, and identity engineering decides how they flow. Contractors need an authoritative source of their own. Gate G1 requires the HR feed working before any rollout. Next, policy.

title: Policy: regenerate Group Policy; don't copy it
say: Group Policy was Active Directory's most ambitious delivery system, and its most network-bound: a client applies it only when it can reach a domain controller. Its replacement is several surfaces: Intune for devices, Conditional Access for access, and Azure machine configuration through Arc for servers, because Intune doesn't manage Windows Server. The program's pattern is regenerate, not copy. Porting a fifty-setting policy as fifty modern settings carries forward dead weight and old conflicts. Microsoft's own recommendation is to start new rather than migrate. A few rules govern every change. Each setting has exactly one owning layer. Require is preferred to block, because a bad block locks people out and a bad require adds a step you can fix. Every change goes through validation and a report-only pilot before production. And the emergency access accounts are excluded from every blocking policy. The decision is the CISO's: the control requirements every surface must meet, meaning the Conditional Access baseline, MFA strength and logging. Gate G1 needs that baseline enforced, with no user outside the MFA requirement except the documented emergency accounts. Next, network services.

title: Network services: DNS, DHCP and IPAM move together
say: Network services are the part organizations most often defer, because DNS, DHCP and address management still work. That's exactly how they keep the old directory alive. The three form one surface. DNS usually lives in zones integrated with Active Directory, so Active Directory can't retire until DNS moves. The forest's DHCP authorization stops an unauthorized Windows server, not a rogue device. And address management, in many organizations, is a spreadsheet one person maintains. Without it, DNS and DHCP drift. So the program moves them together. One governed address management authority covers the whole address surface, on-premises and cloud, and DNS and DHCP derive their records from it. Disagreement between them is drift. The common failure is to modernize identity and policy and leave these for a later phase that rarely happens. A forest that still hosts DNS has not been retired. That makes it a scope and funding decision for the sponsor and the CIO: put DNS, DHCP and IPAM in the core program now, with one IPAM authority. The pilot division's zones move in Phase 2. Next, compute.

title: Compute: the domain join is the last thing to go
say: Once identity, policy and network services have moved, domain-joined machines are the largest remaining dependency. A machine leaves only when its identity, policy and trust have each been replaced, so the domain join is the last thing to go, not the first. User PCs end Entra joined and managed in Intune. Hybrid join is a transition, and there's no supported way to convert a hybrid-joined PC without resetting it, so time that reset to a hardware refresh. Servers take a different road: Azure Arc brings them under policy where they stand, and leaving the domain is decided workload by workload. What really holds servers in the domain is applications. Each Kerberos application is migrated to modern authentication, retired, or, as a last resort, kept on a small documented island with an end-of-life date. And an application's compute stays with its data until its round trips are reduced. Only an application's owner can make that call and sign off its cutover. Keeping legacy authentication open is a risk acceptance, so the authorizing official sets every island and NTLM end date, all resolved by Gate G4. Next, access.

title: Access: log in to applications, not networks
say: When Active Directory retires, being inside the network stops meaning anything. M-22-09 says users should log in to applications rather than networks, and multifactor authentication belongs at the application layer, not in a VPN. The replacement is Zero Trust as the model, Conditional Access deciding each request, a secure access service edge replacing the VPN, and phishing-resistant authentication as the proof. BOD 25-01 makes blocking legacy authentication and phishing-resistant MFA for all users mandatory. FIDO2 keys, passkeys, Windows Hello and PIV or CAC cards qualify; SMS and voice don't. Two consequences need an executive eye. Smart-card sign-in is anchored in Active Directory today. The card and PIN stay, but certificate issuance needs a successor before Active Directory retires. And privilege: every human admin assignment becomes eligible and time-bound, and emergency accounts are tested at least every 90 days. The CISO decides: phishing-resistant MFA as the end state for everyone, Tier 0 administrators first, opening in Phase 1, and certificate issuance moved off AD DS by Gate G4. Next, who leads.

title: Microsoft supplies the instruments, not the orchestra
say: The book's framing is simple. Microsoft provides the instruments; the program provides the orchestra. Cloud identity, device management, Conditional Access and the assessment tools are each excellent. But look at what each one doesn't decide. Cloud identity doesn't decide what your organizational structure should become. The assessment tools don't decide what to do with the findings. Every one of those gaps is a decision someone has to own. And with no vendor deadline forcing it, organizations without leadership migrate in pieces and end up unable to answer last year's audit questions. The program needs no license of its own, but the services it orchestrates do. Federal policy already says this belongs to more than the IT shop. M-22-09 says the whole C-suite must be aligned, and it required a zero trust implementation lead within 30 days. M-19-17 requires an agency-wide identity governance structure that includes HR, general counsel, privacy and acquisition. So the first decision for the sponsor and the CIO, before Phase 0: confirm who already holds those roles, and decide whether one becomes the program's steward. Next, the decision matrix.

title: One decider per decision; the AO signs for risk
say: The book's decision matrix runs on one rule: one decider per row. The single deliberate exception is the pilot gate, G2, which the steward and the sponsor co-sign. The sponsor and the CIO own scope, funding and sequence, break ties, and decide when Active Directory components retire, because each retirement ends a fallback. Their job is to keep this one program, not five projects that finish one at a time. The CISO decides the control requirements. The authorizing official is the only one who can accept risk on the agency's behalf, so every place the program carries risk instead of removing it reaches that desk: a deferred legacy-authentication cutoff, a Kerberos island with no end date, a deviation from a mandatory baseline. The steward's program office runs the orchestra, but it doesn't decide risk or scope. Application owners decide for their applications, and HR decides what the worker attributes mean. The sponsor's decision, before the program starts: fill in the matrix with names, one decider per row, and get the authorizing official's agreement to every risk-acceptance row. Next, three decisions that often land on the wrong desk.

title: Three decisions that land on the wrong desk
say: Three decisions often land on the wrong desk, and the book moves each one on purpose. First, end dates for legacy authentication and NTLM. They sit with the authorizing official, not with the engineers who'd like more time, because keeping legacy authentication open is a risk acceptance, and BOD 25-01 makes blocking it a mandatory baseline. Second, the help desk's identity-verification procedure. The help desk supports users through every wave, and that makes it a target. CISA's advisory on Scattered Spider describes attackers phoning help desks to get passwords reset and MFA moved. So the procedure for resets and temporary access passes is a CISO decision, carried out by the help desk with narrowly scoped roles. Third, records. Retiring Active Directory retires years of access records. NARA's schedule keeps some for six years after an account is terminated, and once a domain controller is gone, its logs can't be recovered. So the records officer decides retention before anything is decommissioned, and the privacy office is consulted before any new attribute flow carries personal data. Now, how to deliver it.

title: Analyze the estate first: read-only, with provenance
say: Delivery starts with the estate. You can't modernize what you haven't enumerated, and nothing can be retired until someone has written down everything it was quietly doing. A long-lived forest usually holds more than anyone on the current team knows: unmapped trusts, Group Policy whose authors left a decade ago, risky certificate templates, and servers past support. The assessment follows three rules. It's read-only, enforced in the account, the code and the audit trail. It's least-privilege, never a domain admin. And every run carries provenance: who ran it, when, against what, and with which rights. The output maps privileged accounts, so it's stored encrypted and handled as sensitive. And because broad enumeration looks like reconnaissance, security operations is told first. One more input decides whether an application may move: how many round trips it makes to its data, measured, not estimated. The steward commissions the assessment in Phase 0. In the program's experience a first pass takes days to a few weeks, and Gate G0 needs it committed. Next, how analysis becomes change.

title: Analyze, plan, deliver: nothing moves without a plan
say: The rule here is simple: nothing touches the target without a plan, and no plan touches it until someone of record has read it. The cycle compares current state with the target, then turns the difference into a plan of small actions, each with its own inverse, so the plan can run backwards. Validation rejects plans that break safety rules, such as deleting too many objects at once. Authorization needs at least one approver who isn't the author. Only then does the execution layer, under a separate identity, deliver and record each action. When something fails, the default is to halt, and every run ends in a signed evidence packet. A separate rule caps how far automation may go, from simply recording up to autonomy for named low-risk classes only. Tenant-wide role changes, Conditional Access enforcement and bulk device changes stay gated permanently. No federal document requires that ceiling; the book chooses it because an authorizing official can sign it. So before the first production delivery, the authorizing official agrees the ceiling for each class of change, with its dry run, approver and rollback on record. Next, the roadmap.

title: The roadmap: seven phases, six gates, five workstreams
say: The roadmap sequences all of this as an illustrative fifty-two-week program. The weeks are a sequencing model, not a commitment; large federal estates typically run multi-year. There are seven phases and six gates. Pre-flight stands up the platform and runs the assessment. Foundation puts identity in place, including the access baseline and the HR feed. A pilot division, typically IT, proves the whole pattern, with zero drift for a hold period. Rollout is the longest phase, division by division. Then legacy retirement, then the shortest phase, retiring AD DS itself, and finally steady state. Two properties define it. The five workstreams run in parallel, each with a named lead, because finishing one before starting the next doubles the duration. And it's gated: a phase opens only when the previous gate clears. The decision closes the loop on ownership. Put the gate dates on the sponsor's calendar, and the end date of every exception on the authorizing official's. Gate G0 gets its date in Phase 0. Next, what makes the gates trustworthy.

title: Gates go green on data, and rollback has an end
say: Two things make the gates trustworthy. First, every gate criterion is evaluated from the repository and the drift reports, not from a signature. Zero drift for fourteen days is a query; so is every PC cloud-joined. A gate the engine can't evaluate needs a better criterion. Second, rollback triggers are thresholds, not judgment calls, and the agency sets the values. Drift above the threshold halts the phase. Conditional Access blocking too many legitimate sign-ins means the policy is reverted. If drift detection stops reporting, all phase work halts. Authority is fixed in advance, from the steward on the early gates to the sponsor and CIO on the last. And be clear about the end. A forest in backup isn't a lasting fallback: a backup is valid only within the tombstone lifetime, 180 days by default. The real rollback point is the last moment a domain controller still runs. So G5 is the sponsor's and the CIO's decision, made on evidence: no live production dependency on Active Directory authentication, or a documented Kerberos island with an end-of-life date. Next, the external clocks.

title: The clocks: FedRAMP's dates don't set the agency's
say: Two external clocks bear on the schedule, and they're easy to confuse. FedRAMP's Consolidated Rules for 2026, announced on June 25, 2026, govern how cloud services are certified. They become mandatory on January 1, 2027, and new Rev5 certification applications stop on June 11, 2027. None of that certifies the agency's own estate. Each agency still authorizes its own systems; what the 2027 date changes is the evidence your providers publish and you inherit. The deadlines that bind the agency directly come from OMB and CISA: M-26-14's logging plan and maturity levels, and BOD 25-01's baselines for Microsoft 365 tenants. The estate has its own dates too. Windows 10 reached end of support on October 14, 2025, Windows Server 2012 security updates ended on October 13, 2026, and Windows Server 2016 reaches end of support on January 12, 2027. Mainframes join the access work late, and may need other zero trust mechanisms. So the sponsor and the CIO sequence the program against the agency's own deadlines and end-of-support dates, starting now, not against FedRAMP's 2027 date. To close, the decisions in one place.

title: Decisions, owners, and where to start
say: So, the decisions, with their owners. Agency leadership and the CIO name the sponsor, the steward and the authorizing official, and the sponsor fills the matrix with one decider per row. The sponsor and the CIO scope all eleven categories, with DNS, DHCP and address management in the core program, and at the end retire Active Directory on evidence. The steward stands up the platform host and commissions the read-only assessment, both in Phase 0. The CISO sets the control requirements, enforced at Gate G1. HR defines what the worker attributes mean. The authorizing official agrees the automation ceiling and every exception's end date. And the records officer settles retention before anything is decommissioned. None of this needs a vendor decision on day one. It needs an inventory, an owner and a date: the read-only assessment, a named sponsor and steward, and Gate G0 on the calendar. Microsoft has supplied the instruments. The program is the orchestra, and the people named in this briefing have to play it. Retiring Active Directory is a governance transformation, and it should be led as one. Book 01 has the detail, with every claim footnoted. Thank you.
